title: Pride And Prejudice: Chapter XXIX
enhanced_title: Pride And Prejudice: Chapter XXIX - The Visit to Rosings
author: Jane Austen
description: This chapter depicts the Bennet party's visit to Rosings Park, where they encounter Lady Catherine de Bourgh in all her magnificence and condescension. The chapter masterfully contrasts the nervous apprehension of Mr. Collins, Maria, and Sir William with Elizabeth Bennet's composed dignity in the face of aristocratic arrogance.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's character is revealed through his excessive admiration for Lady Catherine's 'condescension' in inviting them to dine. His inability to express sufficient wonder at her Ladyship's attention demonstrates his sycophantic nature and his delusion that proximity to aristocracy elevates his own status. Austen uses his triumph to satirize the class-consciousness of the era.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: he knew not how to admire enough.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's composure in the face of Lady Catherine's grandeur stands in sharp contrast to the nervousness of Sir William and Maria Lucas. While others are intimidated by wealth and rank, Elizabeth remains unaffected because she judges character by merit rather than status. This foreshadows her later refusal of Darcy's first proposal, where she will reject his wealth in favor of her principles.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
the mere stateliness of money and rank she
thought she could witness without trepidation.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Austen's description of Lady Catherine makes clear that her authority derives not from any inherent quality but from her position and manner. The detail that whatever she said was spoken in so authoritative a tone as marked her self-importance, and brought Mr. Wickham immediately to Elizabeth's mind, links Lady Catherine's pride to the same family arrogance Elizabeth has already encountered. Elizabeth's calm observation of all three ladies before her reveals the arrogance that she will not bow to.

The stark contrast between mother and daughter—Lady Catherine being tall and commanding while Miss de Bourgh is thin, sickly, and insignificant—suggests the failure of aristocratic breeding to produce worthy heirs. Miss de Bourgh's dependency on Mrs. Jenkinson and her silence throughout the dinner expose the emptiness of a life designed solely for the preservation of wealth and lineage. The detail that Mrs. Jenkinson was entirely engaged in placing a screen in the proper direction before her eyes underscores the daughter's fragility and irrelevance to the social drama unfolding around her.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
who was entirely engaged in listening
to what she said, and placing a screen in the proper direction before
her eyes.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lady Catherine's inquisition of Elizabeth reveals her desire to establish dominance through impertinent questioning about family, education, and accomplishments. Her shock at learning the Bennet sisters were raised without a governess exposes her belief that formal structures are necessary for propriety, insisting that if she had known Elizabeth's mother, she should have advised her most strenuously to engage one. Elizabeth's composed responses show her refusal to be diminished, even as she recognizes the rudeness of the interrogation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
if I had
known your mother, I should have advised her most strenuously to engage
one.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's spirited defense of younger sisters' right to society before their elders marry demonstrates her independent thinking and her commitment to fairness over convention. Lady Catherine's astonishment at Elizabeth's 'decided' opinion marks the clash between Elizabeth's modern sensibility and the aristocratic expectation of deference. The chapter's climax arrives when Elizabeth suspected herself to be the first creature who had ever dared to trifle with so much dignified impertinence, a moment of private triumph that crystallizes her role as Austen's champion of individual merit.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth suspected herself to be the first creature who had ever
dared to trifle with so much dignified impertinence.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The card party scene contrasts the 'superlatively stupid' table of the younger guests with the assertive dominance of Lady Catherine's conversation. Mr. Collins's behavior—agreeing to everything, thanking her for every fish he wins, and apologizing if he thought he won too many—is comically servile and exposes the absurdity of uncritical deference to rank. The chapter ends with Elizabeth politely concealing her true opinion for Charlotte's sake, demonstrating both her loyalty to her friend and her growing sophistication in social navigation, while Mr. Collins was very soon obliged to take her Ladyship's praise into his own hands.

summary: Chapter XXIX presents the memorable visit to Rosings, where Elizabeth Bennet's strength of character is tested against Lady Catherine de Bourgh's aristocratic arrogance. Through satirical portraits of Mr. Collins's sycophancy, Lady Catherine's domineering condescension, and the contrast between the intimidated visitors and Elizabeth's composure, Austen critiques class consciousness while establishing Elizabeth as a heroine who values personal merit over social rank. The chapter's climax comes in Elizabeth's spirited defense of her sisters' right to society and her witty evasion of Lady Catherine's impertinent questions, establishing her as a match for the formidable noblewoman.
